note: How well a given firearm suits a given animal, written by this app from general hunting practice. NOT regulations, NOT CDFW content, NOT sourced to any official publication. Every record deliberately carries no citation field at all — the absence is the honest signal that this is the app's own editorial judgment, and it is rendered on screen as such. No record may state, imply or summarise a rule. Whether a pairing is an authorized method is computed from hunt_methods.json, which is cited, free, and evaluated first: where that file does not authorize a pairing, no grade from this file is rendered. No ballistic quantity anywhere in this file was measured, computed or verified — every tier is editorial judgment.

tips_disclaimer.headline: Equipment notes — not regulations, not CDFW content
tips_disclaimer.body: Written by this app from general hunting practice. Nothing here is a rule and nothing here is permission. What the regulations authorize is answered separately, quoted with its citation on the screen for that animal. A grade here never changes that answer, and a good grade is never shown on a pairing the quoted rule does not cover.
tips_disclaimer.no_citation_line: No citation — this is not sourced to any regulation.

tier_definitions.well_suited: The mainstream choice for this animal in this state. Nothing to explain.
tier_definitions.adequate: Will do the job within its limits. The reason names the limit.
tier_definitions.marginal: Used by some hunters, but leaves little margin for a bad angle or a long shot. The reason must name what has to go right.
tier_definitions.more_than_needed: Effective, but costs recoil, muzzle blast or meat for nothing the animal required. Never a discouragement — the reason should name what the same gun is right for.
tier_definitions.not_suited: We would not recommend this pairing. The reason must name the failure mode, not just say “too small”.

grades.reason: The light end of uncontested, and a mild rifle to shoot well.
Flat, mild and easy to place — a modern take on the same idea as the .243.
Fast and flat, and it holds up in the open country of the north-east.
Enough bullet for deer inside a couple of hundred yards. The limit is distance, not the animal.
The current default, and the recoil is mild enough that most people shoot it better than they shoot bigger rifles.
More case and more recoil than a deer asks for. The same rifle earns it on elk.
Sixty years of California blacktail and mule deer say this one works.
A short, mild cartridge that gives away very little to the bigger sevens on deer.
More reach than a 7mm-08 with the same bullet weight, and still a pleasant rifle to carry.
The brush rifle for coastal blacktail country, and quick to handle in timber.
grades.watch_out: Its arc drops away fast past about 150 yards, so range estimation does more work here than with a flatter cartridge.

grades.reason: The middle of the road for California deer, and it stays useful on pig, bear and elk without changing rifles.
The traditional top of general purpose, and bullets for it are on every shelf.
More recoil, more muzzle blast and more meat damage than a deer asks for. The same rifle is well-suited to elk, and that is where it earns the recoil.
Effective and far more than a deer needs. It comes into its own on elk in open country.
Built for animals several times a deer's weight. On elk and big bear it is the right tool.
Straight-wall bullets do the job inside about 200 yards and the recoil is very mild.
grades.watch_out: It sheds speed quickly. Treat it as a woods cartridge, not an open-country one.

grades.reason: A heavy, slow bullet built for much larger animals. Where it earns its keep is elk and close-cover pig and bear.
Hits hard inside 150 yards and is easy to shoot. Past that the arc falls away fast.
A capable deer revolver inside the ranges a handgun hunter should be taking.
A slow pistol bullet with little penetration for the angles a deer actually presents. The failure mode is a wounded animal at any range a handgun hunter would take.
More recoil than most people can shoot accurately, for an animal a milder revolver already handles.
A big, blunt pistol bullet for an animal that does not need one, and the muzzle blast makes a second shot slow.
Enough for deer with a well-constructed bullet, and it loads light.
What most muzzleloader hunters own, and the bullet selection is the widest.
A heavier ball or bullet than a deer needs, but it shoots flat enough and hits hard.
Effective in brush and close timber. The limit is distance, not power.
Much the same as a 12 in the woods; the harder part is finding the ammunition.
Lighter to carry and easier to shoot than a 12, with a little less reach.
The classic California archery animal, and the seasons are built around it.
Short-range and accurate, and easier to hold steady than a vertical bow.
Enough bullet for heavy shoulder bone at the ranges bear are usually taken.
A heavier bullet than a deer needs, which is exactly what a bear asks for.
The reach and the bullet weight both earn their place here.
Built for this size of animal, and the extra bullet weight buys penetration through bone.
Very effective in close cover. The arc limits it well before the bullet does.
A short-range proposition on an animal that can absorb a poor first shot.
grades.watch_out: Bullet construction matters more here than muzzle energy. A soft bullet that comes apart on the shoulder is the failure mode.

grades.reason: Not enough penetration for the bone a bear puts between the muzzle and the vitals. The failure mode is a wounded animal.
A heavy conical is capable at muzzleloader distances. There is no second shot.
Very effective in thick cover and short on reach.
Effective with good arrow weight and a sharp head, and it asks for patience and a close shot.
grades.watch_out: Blood trails on bear are notoriously poor. Plan the shot around recovery, not around the shot itself.

grades.reason: A proven elk cartridge with a heavy bullet, and mild enough to shoot well.
The traditional elk answer, and it still is.
This is where the recoil is earned — reach and bullet weight both matter here.
Reach and penetration for open country, and bullets built for the job are everywhere.
About as much bullet as anyone needs in California, and it drives through bone.
A heavy conical at close range. One shot, and it has to be the right one.
A close-range proposition on a big animal, and it rewards heavy arrows and a fixed head.
Flat, mild and quick — a good match for a small animal in open country.
Holds its line in the wind, which is the whole problem on the flats.
Flat enough for the ranges pronghorn country offers, without punishing recoil.
More bullet than the animal needs and easy to place, which is the trade most people want.
More recoil and meat damage than a 100-pound animal asks for. The same rifle is well-suited to elk.
Enough bullet for shoulder bone at the ranges California pig country usually gives you.
Heavy bullets, deep penetration, and nothing exotic about the ammunition.
Not overkill here the way it is on a deer — a big boar is worth the extra bullet.
A big, heavy bullet at pig distances, which is what the animal asks for.
Close-cover pig is exactly what this one is for.
A capable close-range revolver with a hard-cast or bonded bullet.
A heavy conical at close range does the job. Plan for one shot.
Hard to beat in thick cover at the distances pigs are usually taken.
Close range, heavy arrow, fixed head.
grades.watch_out: A pig's vitals sit further forward and lower than most people expect, and the shield turns a marginal hit into a lost animal.

grades.reason: The classic rabbit and squirrel rifle. Quiet, cheap, and it does not ruin what you are going to eat.
More reach than a .22 LR for jackrabbits across open ground, at the cost of more damage up close.
Flat and accurate at short range, and the ammunition is hard to find.
Where it earns its keep is distance — it shoots flat enough to make a long jackrabbit shot honest.
grades.watch_out: The same speed that makes it flat makes it destructive on a close cottontail.

grades.reason: More speed than a rabbit needs, and the ammunition costs several times what a .22 LR does.
Fine on a jackrabbit across an open field. On a cottontail at thirty yards there is not much left to carry home.
There is nothing a .308 does for a rabbit that a .22 does not do better and quieter. The same rifle is well-suited to deer, pig, bear and elk.
Enormously more rifle than the animal calls for, and loud enough to end the morning.
A capable revolver aimed at an animal a rimfire handles better and cheaper.
Faster on a moving rabbit than any rifle, and #6 shot over a dog in brush is the standard answer.
Lighter to carry all day and still plenty of pattern for rabbits.
Genuinely fun and genuinely limited — thin patterns mean you have to let them get close.
Quiet and cheap for tree squirrels at close range, and it asks for precise shot placement.
The quiet answer for squirrels and close cottontails, and it carries enough energy to be humane.
More air rifle than a squirrel needs, and heavy to carry for it.
Slow and rewarding, with blunts or judo points to save arrows.
Accurate at short range and slow to reload, which matters more on small game than on deer.
The default for a reason: the widest choice of loads, and enough pattern for turkey as well as quail.
Carries like a 20 and patterns like a 12, and the ammunition is the hard part.
Light to carry over a dog all day, with plenty of pattern for upland birds.
Delightful on quail over a dog, and thin for a big pheasant or a turkey.
A heavy gun built for pass-shooting geese. On quail it is weight you carry for nothing.
Enough for a quail at close range with exact placement, and nothing to spare.
grades.watch_out: Pellet size is not a free choice for turkey — read the quoted rule before you load one.

grades.reason: Rewarding and slow, and the recovery rate is what limits it.
grades.watch_out: Turkey has its own broadhead requirement — read the quoted rule before you fit a field point.

grades.reason: One accurate shot and a slow reload, which suits a blind and not a walk-up.
grades.watch_out: Turkey has its own broadhead requirement — read the quoted rule before you fit a field point.

grades.reason: The default for a reason — the widest choice of nontoxic loads by a distance.
grades.watch_out: Steel #2 to BB is the usual duck load and BBB to T the usual goose load. Those are our suggestions; the ceiling is in the quoted rule.

grades.reason: A heavy gun that swings slowly, bought for pass-shooting geese and rarely needed for ducks over decoys.
Workable on ducks over decoys, and nontoxic loads for it are scarce.
Too few pellets in the pattern for a duck at honest decoy range, and the failure mode is a crippled bird that is never recovered.
This is the pairing where our advice and the pattern board diverge furthest. A .410 nontoxic load puts too few pellets into a pattern to kill a duck cleanly at any honest decoy range.
grades.watch_out: If a .410 is what you have, waterfowl is the wrong quarry for it.

grades.reason: Done by a small number of dedicated hunters, and the recovery rate over water is the reason most do not.
One shot, a slow reload, and a bird that rarely waits. A blind and a lot of patience.

ungraded.why: Opinion on .410 turkey loads has moved sharply with new shot materials and we are not confident enough to grade it. The shot-size limits are in the quoted rule.
On a shielded boar the difference between an adequate hit and a wounded animal is the individual pig, and we do not know enough to tell you which one you will meet.
The same problem as the .410: the outcome turns on the individual animal rather than on the gauge.
